text: Chapter one. What We're Building. Same system, zero code, free tools only.

Here's the truth. You don't need our website to trade like we do. Everything the Market Watch scanner does — regime detection, three-strategy screening, scoring, position tracking — you can do all of it in fifteen minutes a night with tools you already have. Finviz for screening. Google Sheets for tracking. Yahoo Finance for alerts. Zero dollars, zero code, same results. Let me show you exactly how.

Let's put the two versions side by side. Our scanner runs automatically every night at ten thirty. It screens a hundred and sixteen tickers, uses a four-factor composite score, and sends alerts to Telegram. Your D-I-Y version? You do it manually in fifteen minutes. Same tickers via Finviz presets, simplified three-factor scoring, Google Sheets for tracking, Yahoo or Webull for alerts. The core logic is completely identical. The only difference is automation versus fifteen minutes of your time.

Quick quiz before we dive in. How much does the D-I-Y version of this system cost to run? A, ninety-nine dollars a month? B, zero dollars? C, twenty-nine dollars for Finviz Elite? Or D, you need a Bloomberg Terminal? The answer is B. Zero dollars. Finviz free tier. Google Sheets. Yahoo Finance. TradingView free plan. Your only investment is fifteen minutes per evening.
Chapter two. Step one, check market regime. This takes thirty seconds and it changes everything you do next.

The V-I-X is your north star. Below eighteen, you're in Risk-On. Run Momentum and Breakout screens. Eighteen to twenty-two, Neutral. Run all three strategies equally. Twenty-two to twenty-eight, Early Risk-Off. Stick to Oversold and defensive Momentum only. Above twenty-eight, full Risk-Off. Oversold Bounce is your only screen. One number, thirty seconds, completely determines your night. Google V-I-X right now and this table makes perfect sense.

Here's the number one reason D-I-Y screeners blow up. Running momentum screens when the V-I-X is above twenty-eight. Every setup looks clean. Everything looks like a bounce. Then it drops another eight percent the next morning. The regime check takes thirty seconds. Skipping it can cost you a month of gains. Check V-I-X first. Every. Single. Day.

This is S-P-Y, the S and P five hundred E-T-F, and it's your second data point after V-I-X. Is price above or below the fifty-day moving average? That line you see cutting across the chart — that's the S-M-A fifty. Above it means the market is in a structural uptrend. Below it means caution. When both V-I-X is low and S-P-Y is above its fifty-day, you're in the clearest possible Risk-On environment. Pull up this chart every evening alongside your V-I-X check.

Quiz. V-I-X is at thirty-one. S-P-Y is below its fifty-day moving average. Which screener do you run tonight? A, Momentum Expansion because things are cheap? B, Breakout Squeeze because momentum is building? C, Oversold Bounce only because it's Risk-Off? Or D, all three because more signals is better? The answer is C. V-I-X above twenty-eight is full Risk-Off. One screener only. Momentum and Breakout in this regime produce false signals almost every time.
Chapter three. Strategy one, Oversold Bounce. These are quality stocks that got hammered too hard and are ready to snap back.

Here's why oversold bounces work. A large-cap stock with solid fundamentals drops fifteen to twenty percent in a week. Its R-S-I crashes below thirty-five. Statistically, mean reversion kicks in. Institutions start buying the dip, which shows up as a volume spike. You add a market cap floor to filter out speculative garbage. The result is a high-probability bounce setup. The key word here is quality. This only works on real companies with real business behind them, not lottery-ticket micro-caps.

Your Finviz setup for Oversold Bounce. Go to the Technical tab. Set R-S-I fourteen to Oversold, that's below thirty, or Under forty if you want more results. Set Relative Volume to Over one point five. That's fifty percent above normal volume, which tells you institutions are stepping in, not just retail panic. Set Market Cap to Mid or Large, that's two billion dollars and above. No micro-caps. Average Volume over five hundred thousand for enough liquidity to exit cleanly. Save this URL as a bookmark called M-W Oversold.

Look at this X-O-M chart. This is exactly the oversold bounce profile you're hunting. Notice the R-S-I dipping below thirty-five with a clear volume spike on the down day. Large cap, high liquidity, energy sector which is defensive. Then the price stabilizes and bounces. That's mean reversion in action. When you see this pattern in your Finviz results, you're looking at a legitimate candidate. Clean drop, volume on the low, quality company.

Pro tip that saves you five minutes every night. Your Finviz filter settings are stored in the URL. Every time you set up a screen, the URL bar updates with your exact configuration. Bookmark it. Label it M-W Oversold. Do the same for Momentum and Breakout. Tomorrow night, three clicks, three screens loaded instantly. Zero re-entering filters. This sounds trivial but you'll be shocked how much friction it removes from your routine.

Quiz. You find a stock with R-S-I twenty-two, relative volume three point two times normal. Sounds perfect, right? But the market cap is one hundred and eighty million dollars. Do you trade it? A, yes, the signals are perfect? B, no, one-eighty million is a micro-cap with manipulation risk? C, yes, small caps bounce harder? Or D, check earnings first? The answer is B. One hundred and eighty million dollars is a micro-cap. These stocks are easily manipulated, have terrible liquidity, and are frequent pump-and-dump targets. The R-S-I and volume mean nothing without the market cap filter. Quality beats excitement every single time.
Chapter four. Strategy two, Momentum Expansion. This is about buying strength, not weakness. With volume proof that it's real.

Here's the thing that feels counter-intuitive. Most beginners want to buy cheap things. Professionals buy expensive things getting more expensive. A stock trading above its twenty-day moving average with two times normal volume is telling you one thing clearly: big money is committing to this move. The R-S-I between fifty and seventy means the stock is strong but not yet exhausted. There's room to run. This is the bread-and-butter strategy when the V-I-X is below eighteen and everything is green.

Finviz setup for Momentum. Technical tab. Twenty-day S-M-A to Price above S-M-A twenty. That's your uptrend confirmation. Relative Volume over two — double normal volume means money flooding in. R-S-I fourteen to Not Overbought, which gives you that sweet fifty to seventy range. In the Descriptive tab, set Change to Up so you only see green stocks today. Then sort by Relative Volume descending. The highest volume surge stocks come first. Those are your strongest signals. Save as M-W Momentum.

This is N-V-D-A, and it's a textbook momentum expansion example. Price consistently above the twenty-day moving average, which you can see as a line running underneath the candles. Volume surging two to three times on up-days. R-S-I holding in the fifty-five to seventy zone, not overbought. This is what you're looking for in your Finviz results. Strong, steady, institutional. When the next leg up starts, you want to already be on board.

This is critical. Do NOT run the Momentum screen when the V-I-X is above twenty-eight and S-P-Y is below its fifty-day moving average. I know the setups look good. I know the R-S-I and volume check out. But in a Risk-Off regime, momentum screens generate false signals constantly. The stock that looks like it's bouncing drops another ten percent the next day. Check your regime first. Save this strategy for when the market is actually green.

Quiz. A stock is above S-M-A twenty, R-S-I at sixty-five, relative volume two point four times. V-I-X is at fourteen. What do you do? A, skip it because R-S-I sixty-five is almost overbought? B, strong candidate, all signals aligned in Risk-On? C, wait for a pullback to S-M-A twenty? Or D, only trade if it's a tech stock? The answer is B. R-S-I sixty-five is in the momentum sweet spot, not overbought. Above S-M-A twenty, strong volume, V-I-X at fourteen is full Risk-On. Every signal is aligned. This is exactly what you're hunting.
Chapter five. Strategy three, Breakout Squeeze. Stocks that have been coiling tight near resistance and are about to explode through it.

A real breakout looks like this. The stock consolidates below resistance for weeks. Volume dries up. Volatility compresses. Then one day it clears the level on two times normal volume. That's the squeeze releasing. Four things confirm it's real: price above S-M-A fifty, new fifty-two week high, relative volume over one point five, and weekly volatility expanding above three percent. Miss any one of those four and you're probably looking at a fake-out that reverses within days.

Breakout setup in Finviz. Technical tab. Fifty-day S-M-A to Price above S-M-A fifty — medium-term uptrend confirmed. New High to New High — it's breaking out right now. Relative Volume over one point five — institutions are participating. Weekly Volatility over three percent — the squeeze is releasing. Market Cap can be Small, three hundred million and above, or Mid and Large. Breakouts work across all sizes. And always switch to T-A view to visually confirm the consolidation pattern before you commit. Save this as M-W Breakout.

B-T-U is a clean example of the breakout squeeze setup. Look for price consolidating in a tight range below a key level, the S-M-A fifty sloping upward underneath as a support base. Then the stock clears the range on a volume surge. That's not noise — that's institutional commitment. When you see this structure in Finviz's T-A view, you can confirm the setup in literally three seconds without opening another tab. Clean chart, clean break, real volume. That's the criteria.

Quiz. A stock hits a new fifty-two week high. Looks exciting. But relative volume is zero point six — that's below average. Valid breakout? A, yes, new highs are always bullish? B, no, low-volume breakouts reverse constantly? C, yes, volume doesn't matter for breakouts? Or D, wait until tomorrow? The answer is B. Without institutional participation, a breakout has no conviction. The retail momentum fades in days and the stock reverses. Always require relative volume above one point five. New high plus low volume is one of the most common traps in trading.
Chapter six. Scoring and Selection. You've got twenty Finviz results. In ten minutes, you'll narrow it to three A-plus trades.

Three factors, each scored one to three points. Nine points possible. You only trade setups scoring seven or above. Factor one is Technical Setup. Score one if R-S-I is borderline and price barely clears one moving average. Score two for a clear R-S-I signal above one M-A. Score three if R-S-I is perfect and price is above both S-M-A twenty and fifty. Factor two is Volume. One point five to two times is a one. Two to three times is a two. Three times plus is a three — that's institutional flood. Factor three is Chart Clarity. Messy chart is a one. Decent pattern with noise is a two. Textbook clean setup is a three. Add it up. Seven plus, you trade it. Below seven, skip it.

Before you trade any stock from your shortlist, thirty seconds. Non-negotiable. Google the ticker plus the word dilution. Or ticker plus offering. If you see A-T-M offering, warrants, shelf registration, or an S-3 filing from the last ninety days — remove it from your list. Immediately. We learned this the hard way with a ticker called INDO. Technically perfect setup. Beautiful chart. But the S-E-C filings showed toxic financing and warrants that destroyed the stock overnight. The chart couldn't tell you. Google can. Do the check.

Setting your levels is the same structure every single trade. Entry at the previous close or a limit within one percent. Stop loss below the nearest support, typically six to eight percent below entry. T-P-one, where you sell fifty percent, is the next resistance level or ten to fifteen percent up. T-P-two, where you sell the rest, is two times the distance to your stop loss. That's your risk-reward. If it's worse than one point five to one, skip the trade. The math doesn't work. And set a timeout of five trading days. If no exit fires after five days, close at market. No extensions. No hoping.

Quiz. Your screens return twenty results. After scoring, three stocks hit eight out of nine. Seven stocks are in the five to six range. How many do you trade? A, all ten for diversification? B, only the three scoring eight or above? C, the top seven, anything above five is fine? Or D, none, wait for nine out of nine? The answer is B. Three trades. The five-to-six scores lack sufficient confluence. Their win rate is significantly lower than seven-plus setups. Selectivity is your edge. The goal isn't more trades, it's better trades.
Chapter seven. Tracking and your daily routine. Fifteen minutes a night — then you're done, alerts handle the rest.

Exit rules. Burn these into memory. Stop loss fires? Sell immediately. No debate, no hoping, no checking Twitter for opinions. T-P-one fires? Sell fifty percent and move your stop to breakeven. You now have a free trade. T-P-two fires? Sell the rest. Done. Day five timeout? Close at market, whatever the price is. No extensions. Now, when do you do nothing? Price is moving sideways — let the timeout handle it. Down three percent but stop not hit — trust your level. Scary news but the stock is fine — ignore it. A friend tells you to sell — follow your system, not opinions. That's the full framework.

Your evening routine. Fifteen minutes total. Six PM, check V-I-X. Thirty seconds. Google it, note the regime, know which screeners to run. Six oh one, run your Finviz bookmarks. Five minutes. One to three screens based on regime, scan the results. Six oh six, score candidates and dilution check. Five minutes. Chart-check each one, score it, Google ticker plus dilution. Six eleven, update your Google Sheet and set alerts. Four minutes. Log new signals, mark exits, set Yahoo or Webull alerts for stops and T-P-one on every new position. That's it. Alerts handle everything from here.

Based on backtesting, here's what you can realistically expect. Win rate between forty-five and fifty-five percent — meaning roughly half your trades will lose. That's expected. Average win of eight to twelve percent. Average loss of five to seven percent. Notice the asymmetry. Wins are bigger than losses. That's the edge. Monthly return of two to five percent. Not spectacular in isolation. But compounded over twelve months, that's twenty-five to eighty percent. Consistently. Without gambling on earnings or meme stocks.

Your complete D-I-Y scanner checklist. Check V-I-X every evening — thirty seconds, determines everything. Bookmark three Finviz presets. Run regime-appropriate screens only, never all three in Risk-Off. Score each candidate with three factors, trade seven-plus only. Dilution check before any entry. Log everything in Google Sheets. Set alerts for every open position. Position size equals capital divided by four slots, fixed every trade. At T-P-one, sell half and trail stop to breakeven. At day five, close at market. No exceptions, no extensions. That's the whole system.

Final quiz. What's the single biggest advantage of building your own scanner versus paying for a signal service? A, it's cheaper? B, you understand WHY every trade is taken, building real skill? C, you get more signals? Or D, the signals are higher quality? The answer is B. Cost savings are real but secondary. When you build this yourself, you understand the logic behind every trade. When a trade fails, you know exactly why. When the market changes, you adapt. A signal service keeps you dependent. Your D-I-Y system makes you independent. That independence is the actual edge.

Here's the secret professionals never say out loud. They don't win because of better software. They win because they follow a process every single day without exception. Emotion doesn't get a vote. Opinions don't get a vote. The system gets a vote. You now have that system. Three screeners. A scoring sheet. Ironclad exit rules. Fifteen minutes a night. Zero cost. The rest is just discipline. And discipline compounds the same way money does. Start tonight.
